questionMarkup:
The flow depth for a discharge of 10 m3/sm^3/sm3/s in a wide rectangular channel is 2.0 m. Assume that the flow is uniform.

If the discharge is doubled, the flow depth (in m) in this channel is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questionText: The flow depth for a discharge of 10 $m^3/s$ in a wide rectangular channel is 2.0 m. Assume that the flow is uniform.If the discharge is doubled, the flow depth (in m) in this channel is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
Manning's equation for a wide rectangular channel:
Q=1n×A×R2/3×S1/2Q = \dfrac{1}{n} \times A \times R^{2/3} \times S^{1/2}Q=n1​×A×R2/3×S1/2
For wide channel: R≈yR \approx yR≈y (hydraulic radius ≈ depth)
Q=1n×B×y×y2/3×S1/2=BS1/2n×y5/3Q = \dfrac{1}{n} \times B \times y \times y^{2/3} \times S^{1/2} = \dfrac{B S^{1/2}}{n} \times y^{5/3}Q=n1​×B×y×y2/3×S1/2=nBS1/2​×y5/3

So for a wide channel: Q∝y5/3Q \propto y^{5/3}Q∝y5/3 (when B, n, S are constant)

Given: Q1=10m3/sQ_1 = 10m^3/sQ1​=10m3/s at y1=2.0y_1 = 2.0y1​=2.0 m
Q2=20Q_2 = 20Q2​=20 m³/s (doubled)

Ratio:
Q2Q1=(y2y1)5/3\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{y_1}\right)^{5/3}Q1​Q2​​=(y1​y2​​)5/3
2010=(y22.0)5/3\dfrac{20}{10} = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{2.0}\right)^{5/3}1020​=(2.0y2​​)5/3
2=(y22)5/32 = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{2}\right)^{5/3}2=(2y2​​)5/3
y22=23/5=20.6=1.5157\dfrac{y_2}{2} = 2^{3/5} = 2^{0.6} = 1.51572y2​​=23/5=20.6=1.5157
y2=2×1.5157=3.03 my_2 = 2 \times 1.5157 = \mathbf{3.03 \text{ m}}y2​=2×1.5157=3.03 m
explanationText: Manning's equation for a wide rectangular channel: $Q = \dfrac{1}{n} \times A \times R^{2/3} \times S^{1/2}$ For wide channel: $R \approx y$ (hydraulic radius ≈ depth) $Q = \dfrac{1}{n} \times B \times y \times y^{2/3} \times S^{1/2} = \dfrac{B S^{1/2}}{n} \times y^{5/3}$ So for a wide channel: $Q \propto y^{5/3}$ (when B, n, S are constant)Given: $Q_1 = 10m^3/s$ at $y_1 = 2.0$ m $Q_2 = 20$ m³/s (doubled)Ratio: $\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{y_1}\right)^{5/3}$ $\dfrac{20}{10} = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{2.0}\right)^{5/3}$ $2 = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{2}\right)^{5/3}$ $\dfrac{y_2}{2} = 2^{3/5} = 2^{0.6} = 1.5157$ $y_2 = 2 \times 1.5157 = \mathbf{3.03 \text{ m}}$
explanationTex: Q = \dfrac{1}{n} \times B \times y \times y^{2/3} \times S^{1/2} = \dfrac{B S^{1/2}}{n} \times y^{5/3}

questionText: A centrifugal pump is delivering water from an underground tank to an overhead reservoir against a static head of 35 m through a 2 km long, 250 mm diameter pipe. The head-discharge characteristic of the pump is given by $H = 140 - 9000Q^2$ where $H$ is the head (in m) generated by the pump and $Q$ is the discharge (in $m^3/s$ ) of the pump. Neglecting all minor losses, the head (in m) generated by the pump is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).Use: Darcy-Weisbach friction factor $f = 0.04$ , Acceleration due to gravity $= 9.81 m/s^2$ , $\pi = 3.14$
explanationHtml:
Given: Static head =35m,L=2000m,D=250mm=0.25m,f=0.04,g=9.81m/s2,π=3.14= 35 m, L = 2000 m, D = 250 mm = 0.25 m, f = 0.04, g = 9.81 m/s^2, \pi= 3.14=35m,L=2000m,D=250mm=0.25m,f=0.04,g=9.81m/s2,π=3.14
Pump curve: H=140−9000Q2H = 140 - 9000Q^2H=140−9000Q2

Step 1 - Friction head loss (Darcy-Weisbach):
hf=fLV22gD=fL2gD×16Q2π2D4h_f = \dfrac{fLV^2}{2gD} = \dfrac{fL}{2gD} \times \dfrac{16Q^2}{\pi^2 D^4}hf​=2gDfLV2​=2gDfL​×π2D416Q2​...

Using: hf=8fLQ2π2gD5h_f = \dfrac{8fLQ^2}{\pi^2 g D^5}hf​=π2gD58fLQ2​
hf=8×0.04×2000×Q2(3.14)2×9.81×(0.25)5h_f = \dfrac{8 \times 0.04 \times 2000 \times Q^2}{(3.14)^2 \times 9.81 \times (0.25)^5}hf​=(3.14)2×9.81×(0.25)58×0.04×2000×Q2​=640Q29.8596×9.81×0.000977= \dfrac{640 Q^2}{9.8596 \times 9.81 \times 0.000977}=9.8596×9.81×0.000977640Q2​=640Q20.09444= \dfrac{640 Q^2}{0.09444}=0.09444640Q2​=6778Q2= 6778 Q^2=6778Q2

Step 2 - System curve:
Hsys=35+6778Q2H_{sys} = 35 + 6778 Q^2Hsys​=35+6778Q2

Step 3 - Operating point (pump curve = system curve):
140−9000Q2=35+6778Q2140 - 9000Q^2 = 35 + 6778Q^2140−9000Q2=35+6778Q2
105=15778Q2105 = 15778 Q^2105=15778Q2
Q2=10515778=0.006655Q^2 = \dfrac{105}{15778} = 0.006655Q2=15778105​=0.006655
Q=0.08158 m3/sQ = 0.08158 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}Q=0.08158 m3/s

Step 4 - Head generated:
H=140−9000×0.006655=140−59.9=80 mH = 140 - 9000 \times 0.006655 = 140 - 59.9 = \mathbf{80 \text{ m}} H=140−9000×0.006655=140−59.9=80 m
explanationText: Given: Static head $= 35 m, L = 2000 m, D = 250 mm = 0.25 m, f = 0.04, g = 9.81 m/s^2, \pi= 3.14$ Pump curve: $H = 140 - 9000Q^2$ Step 1 - Friction head loss (Darcy-Weisbach): $h_f = \dfrac{fLV^2}{2gD} = \dfrac{fL}{2gD} \times \dfrac{16Q^2}{\pi^2 D^4}$ ...Using: $h_f = \dfrac{8fLQ^2}{\pi^2 g D^5}$ $h_f = \dfrac{8 \times 0.04 \times 2000 \times Q^2}{(3.14)^2 \times 9.81 \times (0.25)^5}$ $= \dfrac{640 Q^2}{9.8596 \times 9.81 \times 0.000977}$ $= \dfrac{640 Q^2}{0.09444}$ $= 6778 Q^2$ Step 2 - System curve: $H_{sys} = 35 + 6778 Q^2$ Step 3 - Operating point (pump curve = system curve): $140 - 9000Q^2 = 35 + 6778Q^2$ $105 = 15778 Q^2$ $Q^2 = \dfrac{105}{15778} = 0.006655$ $Q = 0.08158 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}$ Step 4 - Head generated: $H = 140 - 9000 \times 0.006655 = 140 - 59.9 = \mathbf{80 \text{ m}}$

questionText: The cross section of a 0.5 m wide vertical gate holding water and oil is shown in the figure. The unit weights of water and oil are $10 kN/m^3$ and $7.5 kN/m^3$ , respectively.The horizontal hydrostatic force (in kN) acting on the vertical gate is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
Given: Gate width = 0.5 m; Oil depth = 0.5 m (top); Water depth = 1.0 m (bottom)
γoil=7.5kN/m3,γwater=10kN/m3γ_{oil} = 7.5 kN/m^3, γ_{water} = 10 kN/m^3γoil​=7.5kN/m3,γwater​=10kN/m3

Horizontal hydrostatic force = pressure at centroid x area

Force due to oil layer (0 to 0.5 m depth):
Centroid of oil at depth 0.25 m from oil surface.
Pressure at centroid = γoil×0.25=7.5×0.25=1.875kN/m2\gamma_{oil} \times 0.25 = 7.5 \times 0.25 = 1.875 kN/m^2γoil​×0.25=7.5×0.25=1.875kN/m2
Area = 0.5×0.5=0.25m20.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25 m^20.5×0.5=0.25m2
Foil=1.875×0.25=0.469F_{oil} = 1.875 \times 0.25 = 0.469Foil​=1.875×0.25=0.469 kN

Force due to water layer (0.5 m to 1.5 m depth from oil surface):
Pressure at top of water = γoil×0.5=7.5×0.5=3.75kN/m2\gamma_{oil} \times 0.5 = 7.5 \times 0.5 = 3.75 kN/m^2γoil​×0.5=7.5×0.5=3.75kN/m2
Pressure at bottom = 3.75+γw×1.0=3.75+10=13.75kN/m23.75 + \gamma_w \times 1.0 = 3.75 + 10 = 13.75 kN/m^23.75+γw​×1.0=3.75+10=13.75kN/m2
Average pressure = (3.75+13.75)/2=8.75kN/m2(3.75 + 13.75)/2 = 8.75 kN/m^2(3.75+13.75)/2=8.75kN/m2
Area = 1.0×0.5=0.5m21.0 \times 0.5 = 0.5 m^21.0×0.5=0.5m2
Fwater=8.75×0.5=4.375F_{water} = 8.75 \times 0.5 = 4.375Fwater​=8.75×0.5=4.375 kN

Total force:
F=Foil+Fwater=0.469+4.375=4.84 kNF = F_{oil} + F_{water} = 0.469 + 4.375 = \mathbf{4.84 \text{ kN}}F=Foil​+Fwater​=0.469+4.375=4.84 kN
explanationText: Given: Gate width = 0.5 m; Oil depth = 0.5 m (top); Water depth = 1.0 m (bottom) $γ_{oil} = 7.5 kN/m^3, γ_{water} = 10 kN/m^3$ Horizontal hydrostatic force = pressure at centroid x areaForce due to oil layer (0 to 0.5 m depth):Centroid of oil at depth 0.25 m from oil surface.Pressure at centroid = $\gamma_{oil} \times 0.25 = 7.5 \times 0.25 = 1.875 kN/m^2$ Area = $0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25 m^2$ $F_{oil} = 1.875 \times 0.25 = 0.469$ kNForce due to water layer (0.5 m to 1.5 m depth from oil surface):Pressure at top of water = $\gamma_{oil} \times 0.5 = 7.5 \times 0.5 = 3.75 kN/m^2$ Pressure at bottom = $3.75 + \gamma_w \times 1.0 = 3.75 + 10 = 13.75 kN/m^2$ Average pressure = $(3.75 + 13.75)/2 = 8.75 kN/m^2$ Area = $1.0 \times 0.5 = 0.5 m^2$ $F_{water} = 8.75 \times 0.5 = 4.375$ kNTotal force: $F = F_{oil} + F_{water} = 0.469 + 4.375 = \mathbf{4.84 \text{ kN}}$

Use acceleration due to gravity g=9.8m/s2g = 9.8 m/s^2g=9.8m/s2
questionText: Width (in m) of a rectangular channel required to carry a discharge of $96 m^3/s$ at a critical depth of 9.8 m is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).Use acceleration due to gravity $g = 9.8 m/s^2$
explanationHtml:
At critical depth in a rectangular channel:
Q=Ag⋅ycQ = A\sqrt{g \cdot y_c}Q=Ag⋅yc​​ where A=B×ycA = B \times y_cA=B×yc​ for rectangular channel

Given: Q=96m3/s,yc=9.8m,g=9.8m/s2Q = 96 m^3/s, y_c = 9.8 m, g = 9.8 m/s^2Q=96m3/s,yc​=9.8m,g=9.8m/s2

Formula:
Q=B⋅yc⋅g⋅ycQ = B \cdot y_c \cdot \sqrt{g \cdot y_c}Q=B⋅yc​⋅g⋅yc​​

Solving for B:
B=Qycg⋅yc=969.8×9.8×9.8=969.8×9.8=9696.04≈1.00 mB = \dfrac{Q}{y_c \sqrt{g \cdot y_c}} = \dfrac{96}{9.8 \times \sqrt{9.8 \times 9.8}} = \dfrac{96}{9.8 \times 9.8} = \dfrac{96}{96.04} \approx \mathbf{1.00 \text{ m}}B=yc​g⋅yc​​Q​=9.8×9.8×9.8​96​=9.8×9.896​=96.0496​≈1.00 m
explanationText: At critical depth in a rectangular channel: $Q = A\sqrt{g \cdot y_c}$ where $A = B \times y_c$ for rectangular channelGiven: $Q = 96 m^3/s, y_c = 9.8 m, g = 9.8 m/s^2$ Formula: $Q = B \cdot y_c \cdot \sqrt{g \cdot y_c}$ Solving for B: $B = \dfrac{Q}{y_c \sqrt{g \cdot y_c}} = \dfrac{96}{9.8 \times \sqrt{9.8 \times 9.8}} = \dfrac{96}{9.8 \times 9.8} = \dfrac{96}{96.04} \approx \mathbf{1.00 \text{ m}}$

questionText: In a laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a circular pipe of radius 5 cm, the maximum velocity is found to be 2 m/s. The velocity (in m/s) at a radial distance of 2.50 cm from the axis of the pipe is

options.html: 1.001.001.00
1.251.251.25
1.501.501.50
1.751.751.75

explanationHtml:
Velocity profile for laminar flow in a circular pipe:
v(r)=vmax(1−r2R2)v(r) = v_{max}\left(1 - \dfrac{r^2}{R^2}\right)v(r)=vmax​(1−R2r2​)

Given: R=5R = 5R=5 cm, vmax=2v_{max} = 2vmax​=2 m/s, r=2.5r = 2.5r=2.5 cm

Calculation:
v(2.5)=2×(1−2.5252)=2×(1−6.2525)v(2.5) = 2 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{2.5^2}{5^2}\right) = 2 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{6.25}{25}\right)v(2.5)=2×(1−522.52​)=2×(1−256.25​)
=2×(1−0.25)=2×0.75=1.50 m/s= 2 \times (1 - 0.25) = 2 \times 0.75 = \mathbf{1.50 \text{ m/s}}=2×(1−0.25)=2×0.75=1.50 m/s
explanationText: Velocity profile for laminar flow in a circular pipe: $v(r) = v_{max}\left(1 - \dfrac{r^2}{R^2}\right)$ Given: $R = 5$ cm, $v_{max} = 2$ m/s, $r = 2.5$ cmCalculation: $v(2.5) = 2 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{2.5^2}{5^2}\right) = 2 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{6.25}{25}\right)$ $= 2 \times (1 - 0.25) = 2 \times 0.75 = \mathbf{1.50 \text{ m/s}}$

questionMarkup: For a hydraulic jump formed in a rectangular horizontal channel, the sequent depth ratio is 2. The Froude number of the supercritical stream is:
questionText: For a hydraulic jump formed in a rectangular horizontal channel, the sequent depth ratio is 2. The Froude number of the supercritical stream is:

options.html: 3\sqrt{3}3​
5\sqrt{5}5​
6\sqrt{6}6​
8\sqrt{8}8​

explanationHtml:
Hydraulic jump sequent depth ratio formula:
y2y1=12(−1+1+8Fr12)\dfrac{y_2}{y_1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(-1 + \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}\right)y1​y2​​=21​(−1+1+8Fr12​​)

Given: y2y1=2\dfrac{y_2}{y_1} = 2y1​y2​​=2

Substituting:
2=12(−1+1+8Fr12)2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(-1 + \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}\right)2=21​(−1+1+8Fr12​​)
4=−1+1+8Fr124 = -1 + \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}4=−1+1+8Fr12​​
5=1+8Fr125 = \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}5=1+8Fr12​​
25=1+8Fr1225 = 1 + 8Fr_1^225=1+8Fr12​
Fr12=248=3Fr_1^2 = \dfrac{24}{8} = 3Fr12​=824​=3
Fr1=3Fr_1 = \sqrt{3}Fr1​=3​
explanationText: Hydraulic jump sequent depth ratio formula: $\dfrac{y_2}{y_1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(-1 + \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}\right)$ Given: $\dfrac{y_2}{y_1} = 2$ Substituting: $2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(-1 + \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}\right)$ $4 = -1 + \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}$ $5 = \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}$ $25 = 1 + 8Fr_1^2$ $Fr_1^2 = \dfrac{24}{8} = 3$ $Fr_1 = \sqrt{3}$

questionText: Two reservoirs having different water levels are connected by two long parallel pipelines of same length and same material but having diameters of 600 mm and 400 mm. Q∝D5/2Q \propto D^{5/2}Q∝D5/2

Ratio of flowrates:
Q1Q2=(D1D2)5/2=(600400)5/2=(1.5)5/2\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} = \left(\dfrac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^{5/2} = \left(\dfrac{600}{400}\right)^{5/2} = (1.5)^{5/2}Q2​Q1​​=(D2​D1​​)5/2=(400600​)5/2=(1.5)5/2

questionText: The shaft of a 6 m wide gate in the figure will fail at a moment of 3924 kN.m about the hinge P. The maximum value of water depth $h$ (in m) that the gate can hold is __________ (round off to the nearest integer). Note: Density of water = $1000 , \text{kg/m}^3$ Acceleration due to gravity = $9.81 , \text{m/s}^2$
explanationText: Let Force F acta on a gate at B $\begin{aligned} F & =\rho g \bar{h} A \\ & =\rho g(h-4+2)(5 \times 6) \\ & =1000 \times 9.81 \times(h-2) \times 30 \\ & =294.3 \times(h-2) \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}$ From figure, $\begin{aligned} \sin \theta & =\frac{h-\bar{h}_{c p}}{P B} \\ \frac{4}{5} & =\frac{h-\left[\bar{h}+\frac{I_{C G} \sin ^2 \theta}{A \bar{h}}\right]}{P B} \\ & =\frac{h-\left[h-2+\frac{\frac{6 \times 5^3}{12} \times\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^2}{(h-2) \times 5 \times 6}\right]}{P B} \end{aligned}$ $\Rightarrow \quad P B=\frac{5}{4}\left[2-\frac{4}{3(h-2)}\right]$ Now, taking moment about $P$ , $\begin{aligned} & F \times P B=3924 \\ & 294.3 \times(h-2) \times \frac{5}{4}\left[2-\frac{4}{3(h-2)}\right]=3924 \\ &(h-2) \times\left(2-\frac{4}{3(h-2)}\right)=\frac{32}{3} \\ & 2 h-4-\frac{4}{3}=\frac{32}{3} \\ & h=8 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}$

hf,Bhf,A=f⋅LBDB⋅1DB4f⋅LADA⋅1DA4=LBLA⋅DA5DB5 \frac{h_{f,B}}{h_{f,A}} = \frac{f \cdot \frac{L_B}{D_B} \cdot \frac{1}{D_B^4}}{f \cdot \frac{L_A}{D_A} \cdot \frac{1}{D_A^4}} = \frac{L_B}{L_A} \cdot \frac{D_A^5}{D_B^5} hf,A​hf,B​​=f⋅DA​LA​​⋅DA4​1​f⋅DB​LB​​⋅DB4​1​​=LA​LB​​⋅DB5​DA5​​

explanationText: Given Data (from the figure): Pipe A: $D_A = 2 \ \text{m}, \quad L_A = 100 \ \text{m}, \quad f = 0.01$ Pipe B: $D_B = 1 \ \text{m}, \quad L_B = 200 \ \text{m}, \quad f = 0.01$ Frictional Head Loss Formula (Darcy-Weisbach): $h_f = f \cdot \frac{L}{D} \cdot \frac{v^2}{2g}$ Since discharge is same, velocity is related to diameter: $Q = A \cdot v \Rightarrow v \propto \frac{1}{A} \propto \frac{1}{D^2} \Rightarrow v \propto \frac{1}{D^2}$ So, $v^2 \propto \frac{1}{D^4}$ Ratio of head losses: $\frac{h_{f,B}}{h_{f,A}} = \frac{f \cdot \frac{L_B}{D_B} \cdot \frac{1}{D_B^4}}{f \cdot \frac{L_A}{D_A} \cdot \frac{1}{D_A^4}} = \frac{L_B}{L_A} \cdot \frac{D_A^5}{D_B^5}$ Substitute values: $\frac{h_{f,B}}{h_{f,A}} = \frac{200}{100} \cdot \left( \frac{2}{1} \right)^5 = 2 \cdot 32 = 64$

subject: Fluid Mechanics and Hydraulics
questionMarkup: A hydraulic jump occurs in an open channel when the slope of the channel changes from ______.
questionText: A hydraulic jump occurs in an open channel when the slope of the channel changes from ______.

options.html: MILD slope to STEEP slope
STEEP slope to MILD slope
MILD slope to ZERO slope
STEEP slope to a STEEPER slope
options.text: STEEP slope to a STEEPER slope

explanationHtml:
A hydraulic jump occurs when there is a sudden change in the flow characteristics of the fluid. This phenomenon typically occurs when the flow transitions from a high velocity (steep slope) to a lower velocity (mild slope). The change in slope causes a sudden rise in water level and a loss of kinetic energy, resulting in a turbulent flow downstream.

Thus, the correct answer is (B) STEEP slope to MILD slope.

Given:

g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2g=9.81 m/s2

Step 1: Calculate flow per unit width:
q=Qb=105=2.0 m2/sq = \frac{Q}{b} = \frac{10}{5} = 2.0\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}q=bQ​=510​=2.0 m2/s

yc=(q2g)1/3=(2.029.81)1/3=(0.4077)1/3=0.740 my_c = \left( \frac{q^2}{g} \right)^{1/3} = \left( \frac{2.0^2}{9.81} \right)^{1/3} = (0.4077)^{1/3} = 0.740\ \text{m}yc​=(gq2​)1/3=(9.812.02​)1/3=(0.4077)1/3=0.740 m

Ec=32yc=32⋅0.740=1.11 mE_c = \frac{3}{2} y_c = \frac{3}{2} \cdot 0.740 = 1.11\ \text{m}Ec​=23​yc​=23​⋅0.740=1.11 m

explanationText: Given: Channel width, $b = 5.0\ \text{m}$ Discharge, $Q = 10\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}$ Initial flow depth, $y = 1.5\ \text{m}$ $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$ Step 1: Calculate flow per unit width: $q = \frac{Q}{b} = \frac{10}{5} = 2.0\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}$ Step 2: Critical depth for rectangular channel: $y_c = \left( \frac{q^2}{g} \right)^{1/3} = \left( \frac{2.0^2}{9.81} \right)^{1/3} = (0.4077)^{1/3} = 0.740\ \text{m}$ Step 3: Specific energy at initial condition: $E_1 = y + \frac{v^2}{2g}$ $v = \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{10}{5 \times 1.5} = 1.33\ \text{m/s}$ $E_1 = 1.5 + \frac{(1.33)^2}{2 \cdot 9.81} = 1.5 + \frac{1.7689}{19.62} = 1.5 + 0.0902 = 1.5902\ \text{m}$ Step 4: Specific energy at critical condition: $E_c = \frac{3}{2} y_c = \frac{3}{2} \cdot 0.740 = 1.11\ \text{m}$ Step 5: Bottom raise required: $z = E_1 - E_c = 1.5902 - 1.11 = 0.48\ \text{m}$ Answer: $\boxed{0.48\ \text{m}}$

questionText: For the Bernoulli's equation to be applicable in a fluid flow situation, which of the following conditions is/are to be satisfied:

options.html: Fluid should be frictionless
Fluid should be incompressible
Flow should be steady
Flow should be rotational

explanationHtml:
Bernoulli's equation is applicable under the following assumptions:

(A) Fluid should be frictionless - no energy loss due to viscosity.
(B) Fluid should be incompressible - ρ=constant\rho = \text{constant}ρ=constant
(C) Flow should be steady - ∂∂t=0\frac{\partial}{\partial t} = 0∂t∂​=0
(D) Flow should be rotational - Incorrect, because Bernoulli's equation assumes irrotational flow.

Hence, the correct conditions are:
(A), (B), and (C)
explanationText: Bernoulli's equation is applicable under the following assumptions: (A) Fluid should be frictionless - no energy loss due to viscosity. (B) Fluid should be incompressible - $\rho = \text{constant}$ (C) Flow should be steady - $\frac{\partial}{\partial t} = 0$ (D) Flow should be rotational - Incorrect, because Bernoulli's equation assumes irrotational flow. Hence, the correct conditions are: (A), (B), and (C)

explanationHtml:
Various types of newtonian \& non-newtonian fluids are shown in the figure.
Fluids which obeys Newton's law of viscosity (τ=μdudy) \left(\tau=\mu \frac{\mathrm{du}}{\mathrm{dy}}\right) (τ=μdydu​) are called Newtonian Fluids and those fluids which do not obey this rule are called Non-Newtonian Fluids.
General relationship between shear stress and velocity gradient is given by
τ=A(dudy)n+B \tau=\mathrm{A}\left(\frac{\mathrm{du}}{\mathrm{dy}}\right)^{\mathrm{n}}+\mathrm{B} τ=A(dydu​)n+B
In the figures shown above, slope of the curve is called apparent viscosity.
Fluid for which apparent viscosity increases with du/dy are called Dilatant.
Dilatant fluids are also called shear thickening fluids. Examples of dilatant fluids are solution with suspended starch or sand, sugar in water.
Fluids for which apparent viscosity decreases with du/dy are called Pseudo Plastic.
Pseudo plastic fluid are also called shear thinning fluid. Examples are paints, polymer solutions, blood, paper pulp, syrup, molasses, milk, gelatine.
Bingham Plastic (ideal plastic) fluids require a certain minimum shear stress ty t_{y} ty​ (yield stress) before they start flowing. Examples: tooth paste, sewage sludge, drilling mud have time dependent Newtonian Behaviour.

Fluids which obeys Newton's law of viscosity $\left(\tau=\mu \frac{\mathrm{du}}{\mathrm{dy}}\right)$ are called Newtonian Fluids and those fluids which do not obey this rule are called Non-Newtonian Fluids. General relationship between shear stress and velocity gradient is given by $\tau=\mathrm{A}\left(\frac{\mathrm{du}}{\mathrm{dy}}\right)^{\mathrm{n}}+\mathrm{B}$ In the figures shown above, slope of the curve is called apparent viscosity. Fluid for which apparent viscosity increases with du/dy are called Dilatant. Dilatant fluids are also called shear thickening fluids. Examples of dilatant fluids are solution with suspended starch or sand, sugar in water. Fluids for which apparent viscosity decreases with du/dy are called Pseudo Plastic. Pseudo plastic fluid are also called shear thinning fluid. Examples are paints, polymer solutions, blood, paper pulp, syrup, molasses, milk, gelatine. Bingham Plastic (ideal plastic) fluids require a certain minimum shear stress $t_{y}$ (yield stress) before they start flowing. Examples: tooth paste, sewage sludge, drilling mud have time dependent Newtonian Behaviour.

explanationHtml:
In case of discrete particle settling and Stoke's law valid, at terminal velocity, since there is no change in velocity, the net force on the body is zero. Hence,


FD=(π6D3ρsg−π6D3ρsg)=π6gD3(ρs−ρf)F_D=\left ( \frac{\pi}{6}D^3\rho _sg-\frac{\pi}{6}D^3\rho _sg \right )=\frac{\pi}{6}gD^3(\rho _s-\rho _f) FD​=(6π​D3ρs​g−6π​D3ρs​g)=6π​gD3(ρs​−ρf​)
For density of medium (ρf)(\rho _f) (ρf​) and mass density of sphere (ρs)(\rho _s) (ρs​) constant,
Drag force (FD)∝D3(F_D)\propto D^3 (FD​)∝D3

⇒(FD)Q(FD)P=(DQ)3(DP)3=(10.5)3=8\Rightarrow \frac{(F_D)_Q}{(F_D)_P}=\frac{(D_Q)^3}{(D_P)^3}=\left ( \frac{1}{0.5} \right )^3=8 ⇒(FD​)P​(FD​)Q​​=(DP​)3(DQ​)3​=(0.51​)3=8

explanationText: In case of discrete particle settling and Stoke's law valid, at terminal velocity, since there is no change in velocity, the net force on the body is zero. Hence, $F_D=\left ( \frac{\pi}{6}D^3\rho _sg-\frac{\pi}{6}D^3\rho _sg \right )=\frac{\pi}{6}gD^3(\rho _s-\rho _f)$ For density of medium $(\rho _f)$ and mass density of sphere $(\rho _s)$ constant, Drag force $(F_D)\propto D^3$ For particle P, diameter $(D_P)=0.5 mm$ For particle Q, diameter $(D_Q)=1 mm$ $\Rightarrow \frac{(F_D)_Q}{(F_D)_P}=\frac{(D_Q)^3}{(D_P)^3}=\left ( \frac{1}{0.5} \right )^3=8$ $\Rightarrow (F_D)_Q=8 \times (F_D)P$

questionText: A 1 m wide rectangular channel carries a discharge of 2 $m^{3}/s$ . The specific energy-depth diagram is prepared for the channel. explanationHtml:
Let Supercritical depth =Y
Subcritical depth =2 Y
As the specific energy E remains constant for alternate depths
∴E1=E2⇒Y1+Q22gB2Y12=Y2+Q22gB2Y22⇒Y+222×9.81×12×(Y)2=2Y+222×9.81×1×(2Y)2Y+0.204Y2=2Y+0.051Y2⇒Y=0.204−0.051Y2=Y⇒Y3=0.1530⇒Y=0.534∴Subcritical depth=0.534×2=1.0697≃1.07m \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad E_{1}&=E_{2} \\ \Rightarrow Y_{1}+\frac{Q^{2}}{2 g B^{2} Y_{1}^{2}}&=Y_{2}+\frac{Q^{2}}{2 g B^{2} Y_{2}^{2}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad Y+\frac{2^{2}}{2 \times 9.81 \times 1^{2} \times( Y)^{2}}&=2 Y+\frac{2^{2}}{2 \times 9.81 \times 1 \times(2 Y)^{2}} \\ Y+\frac{0.204}{Y^{2}}&=2Y+\frac{0.051}{Y^{2}}\\ \Rightarrow \quad Y=\frac{0.204-0.051}{Y^{2}}&=Y \\ \Rightarrow \quad Y^{3}&=0.1530 \\ \Rightarrow \quad Y&=0.534 \\ \therefore \quad \text{Subcritical depth} \\ &=0.534 \times 2 \\ &=1.0697 \\ &\simeq 1.07 \mathrm{m} \\ \end{aligned}∴E1​⇒Y1​+2gB2Y12​Q2​⇒Y+2×9.81×12×(Y)222​Y+Y20.204​⇒Y=Y20.204−0.051​⇒Y3⇒Y∴Subcritical depth​=E2​=Y2​+2gB2Y22​Q2​=2Y+2×9.81×1×(2Y)222​=2Y+Y20.051​=Y=0.1530=0.534=0.534×2=1.0697≃1.07m​
explanationText: Let Supercritical depth =Y Subcritical depth =2 Y As the specific energy E remains constant for alternate depths $\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad E_{1}&=E_{2} \\ \Rightarrow Y_{1}+\frac{Q^{2}}{2 g B^{2} Y_{1}^{2}}&=Y_{2}+\frac{Q^{2}}{2 g B^{2} Y_{2}^{2}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad Y+\frac{2^{2}}{2 \times 9.81 \times 1^{2} \times( Y)^{2}}&=2 Y+\frac{2^{2}}{2 \times 9.81 \times 1 \times(2 Y)^{2}} \\ Y+\frac{0.204}{Y^{2}}&=2Y+\frac{0.051}{Y^{2}}\\ \Rightarrow \quad Y=\frac{0.204-0.051}{Y^{2}}&=Y \\ \Rightarrow \quad Y^{3}&=0.1530 \\ \Rightarrow \quad Y&=0.534 \\ \therefore \quad \text{Subcritical depth} \\ &=0.534 \times 2 \\ &=1.0697 \\ &\simeq 1.07 \mathrm{m} \\ \end{aligned}$

options.text: Fluid is compressible and flow is irrotational

explanationHtml:
Continuity equation
∂u∂x+∂v∂y=0⇒(2−2xy)+(2xy−2)=00=0 \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y} &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad(2-2 x y)+(2 x y-2) &=0 \\ 0 &=0 \end{aligned}∂x∂u​+∂y∂v​⇒(2−2xy)+(2xy−2)0​=0=0=0​
Hence, incompressible fluid.
ωz=12[∂v∂x−∂u∂y]=12[y2−3x23−(3y23−x2)]=12[y2−x2−y2+x2]=0 \begin{aligned} \omega_{z} &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[y^{2}-\frac{3 x^{2}}{3}-\left(\frac{3 y^{2}}{3}-x^{2}\right)\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[y^{2}-x^{2}-y^{2}+x^{2}\right] \\ &=0 \end{aligned}ωz​​=21​[∂x∂v​−∂y∂u​]=21​[y2−33x2​−(33y2​−x2)]=21​[y2−x2−y2+x2]=0​
Hence, flow is irrotational.
explanationText: Continuity equation $\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y} &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad(2-2 x y)+(2 x y-2) &=0 \\ 0 &=0 \end{aligned}$ Hence, incompressible fluid. $\begin{aligned} \omega_{z} &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[y^{2}-\frac{3 x^{2}}{3}-\left(\frac{3 y^{2}}{3}-x^{2}\right)\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[y^{2}-x^{2}-y^{2}+x^{2}\right] \\ &=0 \end{aligned}$ Hence, flow is irrotational.

questionText: A rectangular channel 6.0 m wide carries a discharge of 16.0 $m^{3}/s$ under uniform flow condition with normal depth of 1.60 m. Minning's n is 0.015. The channel width is to be contracted. The minimum width to which the channel can be contracted without affecting the upstream flow condition is

options.html: 3m

explanationHtml:
Fr=VC0= Flow speed  Wave speed F_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{V}{C_{0}}=\frac{\text { Flow speed }}{\text { Wave speed }}Fr​=C0​V​= Wave speed  Flow speed ​
At low speed, Ft<1;F_{t} \lt 1;Ft​<1; a small disturbance travels u/s (with a velocity C0−VC_{0}-VC0​−V relative to a stationary observer) and affects the u/s conditions.
At high flow velocities, Fr>1F_{r} \gt 1Fr​>1, a small disturbance travels d/s at a velocity of V−C0\mathrm{V}-\mathrm{C}_{0}V−C0​ relative to a stationary observer. explanationText: For equation of stream line in two dimensions is given as $\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial U}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial V}{\partial y}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 1.5+\frac{\partial V}{\partial y} &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}&=-1.5 \\ \Rightarrow \quad v&=-1.5 \mathrm{y}+\mathrm{C}\\ \text { But at } \quad y&=0, v=0\\ \therefore \quad 0&=-15 \times 0+C \\ \Rightarrow \quad C&=0\\ \text { Thus } \quad v&=-1.5 \mathrm{y} \end{aligned}$

The solid sphere will be acted upon by three forces viz. drag force (FD)\left(\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{D}}\right)(FD​), force of buoyancy (FB)\left(\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}}\right)(FB​) and self weight of sphere (W)

questionText: Two pipelines, one carrying oil (mass density 900 kg/ $m^{3}$ ) and the other water, are connected to a manometer as shown in figure. By what amount the pressure in the water pipe should be increased so that the mercury levels in both the limbs of the manometer become equal ? explanationHtml:
Initially the pressure difference between water and oil can be given as


pw+(1000×9.81×1.5)+(13550×9.81×20×10−2)−(900×9.81×3)=p0⇒  pwt+14715+26585.1−26487=p0⇒p0−pw=14813.1⇒P0−Pw=14.8kPa…(i) \begin{aligned} p_{w}+(1000 &\times 9.81 \times 1.5)+(13550 \times 9.81 \times 20 \\ \left.\times 10^{-2}\right)-(900 &\times 9.81 \times 3)=p_{0}\\ \Rightarrow \; p_{w t}+14715+26585.1-26487=p_{0} \\ \Rightarrow \quad p_{0}-p_{w}&=14813.1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad P_{0}-P_{w}&=14.8 \mathrm{kPa} &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}pw​+(1000×10−2)−(900⇒pwt​+14715+26585.1−26487=p0​⇒p0​−pw​⇒P0​−Pw​​×9.81×1.5)+(13550×9.81×20×9.81×3)=p0​=14813.1=14.8kPa​…(i)​
To make the same level of mercury in both the limbs, the level of mercury should be decreased by 10 cm in right limb and increased by 10cm in lett limb
Pwt+(1000×9.81×1.6)−(900×9.81×2.9)=p0⇒P0−pwt=−9.9kPa…(ii) \begin{aligned} P_{w t}+(1000 \times 9.81 &\times 1.6)-(900 \times 9.81 \times 2.9)=p_{0}\\ \Rightarrow \quad P_{0}-p_{w t}&=-9.9 \mathrm{kPa} &\ldots(ii)\\ \end{aligned}Pwt​+(1000×9.81⇒P0​−pwt​​×1.6)−(900×9.81×2.9)=p0​=−9.9kPa​…(ii)​
Subtracting (ii) from (i) we get
PW−PN=14.8+99Pwt−Pw=24.7kPa (increase)  \begin{array}{l} P_{W}-P_{N}=14.8+99 \\ P_{\mathrm{w} t}-P_{\mathrm{w}}=24.7 \mathrm{kPa} \text { (increase) } \end{array}PW​−PN​=14.8+99Pwt​−Pw​=24.7kPa (increase) ​
explanationText: Initially the pressure difference between water and oil can be given as $\begin{aligned} p_{w}+(1000 &\times 9.81 \times 1.5)+(13550 \times 9.81 \times 20 \\ \left.\times 10^{-2}\right)-(900 &\times 9.81 \times 3)=p_{0}\\ \Rightarrow \; p_{w t}+14715+26585.1-26487=p_{0} \\ \Rightarrow \quad p_{0}-p_{w}&=14813.1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad P_{0}-P_{w}&=14.8 \mathrm{kPa} &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}$ To make the same level of mercury in both the limbs, the level of mercury should be decreased by 10 cm in right limb and increased by 10cm in lett limb $\begin{aligned} P_{w t}+(1000 \times 9.81 &\times 1.6)-(900 \times 9.81 \times 2.9)=p_{0}\\ \Rightarrow \quad P_{0}-p_{w t}&=-9.9 \mathrm{kPa} &\ldots(ii)\\ \end{aligned}$ Subtracting (ii) from (i) we get $\begin{array}{l} P_{W}-P_{N}=14.8+99 \\ P_{\mathrm{w} t}-P_{\mathrm{w}}=24.7 \mathrm{kPa} \text { (increase) } \end{array}$

questionText: A hydraulic jump takes place in a triangular channel of vertex angle 90 $^{\circ}$ , as shown in figure. The discharge is 1 $m^{3}/s$ and the pre-jump depth is 0.5 m. What will be the post-jump depth ? (Take g = 981 $m/s^{2}$ )
explanationHtml:
Specific force will remain constant on both sides of hydraulic jump.
∴Q2gA1+A1Zˉ1=Q2gA2+A2Zˉ2A1=y12;A2=y22Zˉ1=(y13);Zˉ2=(y23)GivenQ=1m3/s;y1=0.5m∴(1)29.81×(0.5)2+(0.5)2×(0.53)=(1)29.81×y22+(y2)2×(y23)⇒0.4494=0.1019y22+y233 \begin{aligned} \therefore \frac{Q^{2}}{g A_{1}}+A_{1} \bar{Z}_{1} &=\frac{Q^{2}}{g A_{2}}+A_{2} \bar{Z}_{2} \\ A_{1} &=y_{1}^{2} ; A_{2}=y_{2}^{2} \\ \bar{Z}_{1} &=\left(\frac{y_{1}}{3}\right) ; \quad \bar{Z}_{2}=\left(\frac{y_{2}}{3}\right) \\ \text{Given}\quad Q &=1 \mathrm{m}^{3 / \mathrm{s}} ; y_{1}=0.5 \mathrm{m}\\ \therefore \frac{(1)^{2}}{9.81 \times(0.5)^{2}}&+(0.5)^{2} \times\left(\frac{0.5}{3}\right) \\ &=\frac{(1)^{2}}{9.81 \times y_{2}^{2}}+\left(y_{2}\right)^{2} \times\left(\frac{y_{2}}{3}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.4494&=\frac{0.1019}{y_{2}^{2}}+\frac{y_{2}^{3}}{3} \\ \end{aligned}∴gA1​Q2​+A1​Zˉ1​A1​Zˉ1​GivenQ∴9.81×(0.5)2(1)2​⇒0.4494​=gA2​Q2​+A2​Zˉ2​=y12​;A2​=y22​=(3y1​​);Zˉ2​=(3y2​​)=1m3/s;y1​=0.5m+(0.5)2×(30.5​)=9.81×y22​(1)2​+(y2​)2×(3y2​​)=y22​0.1019​+3y23​​​
By hit and trial, we get y2=1.02my_{2}=1.02 \mathrm{m}y2​=1.02m
explanationText: Specific force will remain constant on both sides of hydraulic jump. $\begin{aligned} \therefore \frac{Q^{2}}{g A_{1}}+A_{1} \bar{Z}_{1} &=\frac{Q^{2}}{g A_{2}}+A_{2} \bar{Z}_{2} \\ A_{1} &=y_{1}^{2} ; A_{2}=y_{2}^{2} \\ \bar{Z}_{1} &=\left(\frac{y_{1}}{3}\right) ; \quad \bar{Z}_{2}=\left(\frac{y_{2}}{3}\right) \\ \text{Given}\quad Q &=1 \mathrm{m}^{3 / \mathrm{s}} ; y_{1}=0.5 \mathrm{m}\\ \therefore \frac{(1)^{2}}{9.81 \times(0.5)^{2}}&+(0.5)^{2} \times\left(\frac{0.5}{3}\right) \\ &=\frac{(1)^{2}}{9.81 \times y_{2}^{2}}+\left(y_{2}\right)^{2} \times\left(\frac{y_{2}}{3}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.4494&=\frac{0.1019}{y_{2}^{2}}+\frac{y_{2}^{3}}{3} \\ \end{aligned}$ By hit and trial, we get $y_{2}=1.02 \mathrm{m}$

options.html: 15∘^{\circ}∘
30∘^{\circ}∘
45∘^{\circ}∘
60∘^{\circ}∘

explanationHtml:
From continuity equation, we get,
Q0=Q1+Q2⇒Q0=0.25Q0+Q2⇒Q2=0.75Q0 \begin{aligned} & & Q_{0}=Q_{1}+Q_{2} \\ \Rightarrow & & Q_{0}=0.25 Q_{0}+Q_{2} \\ \Rightarrow & & Q_{2}=0.75 Q_{0} \end{aligned}⇒⇒​​Q0​=Q1​+Q2​Q0​=0.25Q0​+Q2​Q2​=0.75Q0​​
since, the impact losses are neglected, the velocity will remain unchanged in the direction of Q1 Q_{1}Q1​ and Q2Q_{2} Q2​
i.e.,V0=V1=V2 \text{i.e.},\quad V_{0}=V_{1}=V_{2} i.e.,V0​=V1​=V2​
Applying impulse momentum equation, we get,
ρQ0V0sin⁡θ=ρQ2V2−ρQ1V1⇒Q0sin⁡θ=0.75Q0−0.25Q0⇒sin⁡θ=1/2⇒θ=30∘ \begin{aligned} \rho Q_{0} V_{0} \sin \theta&=\rho Q_{2} V_{2}-\rho Q_{1} V_{1} \\ \Rightarrow \quad Q_{0} \sin \theta&=0.75 Q_{0}-0.25 Q_{0} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \sin \theta&=1 / 2 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \theta&=30^{\circ} \end{aligned}ρQ0​V0​sinθ⇒Q0​sinθ⇒sinθ⇒θ​=ρQ2​V2​−ρQ1​V1​=0.75Q0​−0.25Q0​=1/2=30∘​
explanationText: From continuity equation, we get, $\begin{aligned} & & Q_{0}=Q_{1}+Q_{2} \\ \Rightarrow & & Q_{0}=0.25 Q_{0}+Q_{2} \\ \Rightarrow & & Q_{2}=0.75 Q_{0} \end{aligned}$ since, the impact losses are neglected, the velocity will remain unchanged in the direction of $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ $\text{i.e.},\quad V_{0}=V_{1}=V_{2}$ Applying impulse momentum equation, we get, $\begin{aligned} \rho Q_{0} V_{0} \sin \theta&=\rho Q_{2} V_{2}-\rho Q_{1} V_{1} \\ \Rightarrow \quad Q_{0} \sin \theta&=0.75 Q_{0}-0.25 Q_{0} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \sin \theta&=1 / 2 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \theta&=30^{\circ} \end{aligned}$

questionText: A laboratory model of a river is built to a geometric scale of 1:100. The fluid used in the model is oil of mass density 900 kg/ $m^{3}$ . The highest flood in the river is 10,000 $m^{3}$ /s. The corresponding discharge in the model shall be

options.html: 0.095m3/sm^{3}/sm3/s
0.100m3/sm^{3}/sm3/s
0.105m3/sm^{3}/sm3/s
10.5m3/sm^{3}/sm3/s

explanationHtml:
Froude model law will be applicable in this case.
QmQp=(Lm)3/Tm(Lp)3/TD[∵LmTm=Vm]⇒QmQp=Vm(Lm)2Vp(Lp)2[∵v1=L]⇒QmQp=(LmLD)5/2⇒Qm=Qp×(LmLp)5/2⇒Qm=10.000×(1100)5/2=0.1m3/s \begin{aligned} \frac{Q_{m}}{Q_{p}}&=\frac{\left(L_{m}\right)^{3} / T_{m}}{\left(L_{p}\right)^{3} / T_{D}} \qquad\left[\because \frac{L_{m}}{T_{m}}=V_{m}\right]\\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{Q_{m}}{Q_{p}}&=\frac{V_{m}\left(L_{m}\right)^{2}}{V_{p}\left(L_{p}\right)^{2}} \quad\left[\because v_{1}=\sqrt{L}\right] \\ \Rightarrow \frac{Q_{m}}{Q_{p}}&=\left(\frac{L_{m}}{L_{D}}\right)^{5 / 2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad Q_{m}&=Q_{p} \times\left(\frac{L_{m}}{L_{p}}\right)^{5 / 2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad Q_{m}&=10.000 \times\left(\frac{1}{100}\right)^{5 / 2} \\ &=0.1 \mathrm{m}^{3}/s \end{aligned}Qp​Qm​​⇒Qp​Qm​​⇒Qp​Qm​​⇒Qm​⇒Qm​​=(Lp​)3/TD​(Lm​)3/Tm​​[∵Tm​Lm​​=Vm​]=Vp​(Lp​)2Vm​(Lm​)2​[∵v1​=L​]=(LD​Lm​​)5/2=Qp​×(Lp​Lm​​)5/2=10.000×(1001​)5/2=0.1m3/s​
explanationText: Froude model law will be applicable in this case. $\begin{aligned} \frac{Q_{m}}{Q_{p}}&=\frac{\left(L_{m}\right)^{3} / T_{m}}{\left(L_{p}\right)^{3} / T_{D}} \qquad\left[\because \frac{L_{m}}{T_{m}}=V_{m}\right]\\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{Q_{m}}{Q_{p}}&=\frac{V_{m}\left(L_{m}\right)^{2}}{V_{p}\left(L_{p}\right)^{2}} \quad\left[\because v_{1}=\sqrt{L}\right] \\ \Rightarrow \frac{Q_{m}}{Q_{p}}&=\left(\frac{L_{m}}{L_{D}}\right)^{5 / 2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad Q_{m}&=Q_{p} \times\left(\frac{L_{m}}{L_{p}}\right)^{5 / 2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad Q_{m}&=10.000 \times\left(\frac{1}{100}\right)^{5 / 2} \\ &=0.1 \mathrm{m}^{3}/s \end{aligned}$
